The new statement names two direct borrows of s, matching the Book's r1/r2 example (E0499, 'first borrow later used here'). Source moved to the Book page that shows it. (final: keep)
rust-fundamentals-sr2-04.statement: `let a = &mut s; let b = &mut s;` compiles when `a` is still used after `b` is created.
rust-fundamentals-sr2-04.explanation: The first mutable borrow of s stays live until a's last use, so creating b in the meantime is a second simultaneous &mut borrow, which the borrow checker rejects.
rust-fundamentals-sr2-04.misconception: A second mutable borrow of the same value is fine while the first one is still used later.

rust-fundamentals-sr5-07.statement: A second inherent `impl` block can replace a struct's previously defined methods.
rust-fundamentals-sr5-07.explanation: Inherent impl blocks for one type add their items together. Reusing a method name that an earlier impl block of the type already defines is a duplicate definition the compiler rejects.
rust-fundamentals-sr5-07.misconception: A later inherent impl block overwrites the type's previously defined methods.

Now one direction is concrete: a value known only as FnOnce passed where Fn is required. (final: keep)
rust-fundamentals-sr10-04.statement: Inside `fn run<F: FnOnce()>(f: F)`, passing `f` to a parameter bounded by `Fn()` compiles.
rust-fundamentals-sr10-04.explanation: Fn has FnMut and FnOnce as supertraits, so every Fn type also satisfies FnOnce. A type known only to be FnOnce gives no Fn guarantee, so the call is rejected.
rust-fundamentals-sr10-04.misconception: A FnOnce bound is enough to satisfy an Fn bound because the closure traits form a supertrait chain.

rust-fundamentals-sr1-04.statement: When code assigns a new `String` to `s`, Rust frees the old buffer at the end of `s`'s scope.
rust-fundamentals-sr1-04.explanation: Replacing an existing String drops its previous value immediately. Its old allocation is released during the assignment.
